objections.objection: The draft claims KEYNOTE-054 'has posted an overall-survival result that carries no statistical analysis at all,' but the KEYNOTE-054 registry (NCT02362594) shows overall survival as NOT_POSTED with an anticipated posting date of November 2026.
objections.quote: KEYNOTE-054 and KEYNOTE-716 are both pembrolizumab against placebo; each lists overall survival as a secondary endpoint, and each has posted an overall-survival result that carries no statistical analysis at all — no hazard ratio, no confidence interval, no p-value.
objections.why: The KEYNOTE-054 registry record (NCT02362594) lists overall survival reporting status as NOT_POSTED, directly contradicting the claim that a result has been posted. If KEYNOTE-054 has not posted an OS result at all, the sentence is factually wrong about what was released, and the same question applies to KEYNOTE-716. The error matters because it mischaracterises the state of the OS evidence for the comparison arm's drug class — the actual situation (no OS result posted) is more extreme than what the draft describes (an OS result posted without statistics).
objections.fix: Replace 'each has posted an overall-survival result that carries no statistical analysis at all' with 'neither has posted an overall-survival result' if that is what the registry records show, or cite the specific conference presentation or publication where each OS result appears and describe what statistical analysis it did or did not carry.

objections.objection: The draft characterises Morning Glory Sciences as 'a site publishing this article in English translation,' implying the original was in another language, without stating what language or offering any evidence for this characterisation.
objections.quote: Morning Glory Sciences — a site publishing this article in English translation, and one we can find no other publication citing
objections.why: The phrase 'in English translation' is a claim about the site's publishing practice — that the article was originally written in another language and translated. No source or language of origin is given. If this is wrong, it mischaracterises the outlet. The draft already discounts the outlet's authority; adding an unverified claim about translation compounds the characterisation without evidence.
objections.fix: Remove 'in English translation' unless the original language and translation can be identified, or replace with a neutral description such as 'a site we can find no other publication citing.'

objections.objection: The draft says the Phase 3 is 'seven times larger' than the Phase 2b, but 1,137 divided by 157 is 7.24, making 'more than seven times larger' the more precise statement.
objections.quote: It is the more trustworthy trial by a wide margin — seven times larger, and blinded against the direction the earlier trial's assessment bias could run in.
objections.why: The ratio is 7.24, so 'seven times larger' understates the difference slightly. In a piece that is precise about every other number, this rounding in the unflattering direction (making the Phase 3 sound smaller relative to the Phase 2b than it is) is a minor calibration issue rather than a material error, but it is the kind of imprecision this publication says it avoids.
objections.fix: Change 'seven times larger' to 'more than seven times larger' or 'roughly seven times larger.'

objections.objection: The draft says the survival analysis rests on 'fourteen deaths, seven in each arm' in the short version summary box, but the same section later clarifies that 'n=14' means fourteen deaths among 157 patients — the summary box does not give the denominator, leaving a reader to wonder whether fourteen is the total patient count or the death count.
objections.why: The summary box entry '14 deaths the whole survival analysis' is accurate but compressed. A reader who reads only the summary box does not know that these fourteen deaths are drawn from 157 patients, which is the fact that makes the interval so wide. The body explains this clearly; the summary box does not. This is a calibration issue, not a factual error.
objections.fix: Expand the summary box entry to '14 deaths (of 157 patients) the whole survival analysis' or add a parenthetical such as '(7 per arm, 157 patients total).'

objections.objection: The draft says 'the release says so' about the hazard ratios belonging to KEYNOTE-942, but the short version also says 'the release says so' — these are two separate instances of the same claim and both are accurate, but the second instance in the body section is the one that does the evidential work and should be the one a reader can check.

No objection on substance; flagged only because the short version makes this claim without a citation, while the body section provides the supporting detail. This is a structural note, not a correction.

However, the three-year figure of 62% is stated without a source citation in this sentence, while the five-year figure of 59% is sourced. That arithmetic is correct. The upper bound of HR 1.345 means the treated group's hazard of death is about 34.5% higher — 'about a third higher' is a reasonable approximation. Both ends are correctly described as rate comparisons. No finding.

inferences.quote: the study will continue in order to evaluate other key secondary endpoints, including overall survival

The Merck/Moderna press release and the ASCO Post both describe DMFS as 'a key secondary endpoint' and list OS simply as a secondary endpoint. Calling OS a 'key secondary endpoint' in this sentence overstates its pre-specified hierarchical status relative to DMFS, which was the designated key secondary.

inferences.quote: A one-sided test asks only 'is it better?' A two-sided test asks 'is it different, in either direction?' For a symmetric test the two-sided p-value is about double the one-sided one, so the same data gives 0.0266 one way and 0.053 the other — identical evidence, measured against a different question.
inferences.problem: The relationship 'two-sided p ≈ 2 × one-sided p' holds only when the one-sided test is in the direction of the observed effect. The draft states this as a general rule without that qualification, which could mislead a reader into thinking the doubling is always exact or always applies. This is a minor calibration issue, not a serious error, but the omission of the directionality condition leaves the explanation incomplete.
inferences.correct_reading: The two-sided p-value is approximately double the one-sided p-value when the one-sided test is in the direction of the observed effect (i.e., when the point estimate favours the treatment). The draft's arithmetic is correct for this case but the condition should be stated.
inferences.fix: Add after 'about double the one-sided one': '(when the one-sided test is in the direction of the observed effect, as it is here)'.

inferences.quote: The confidence interval is the tell: 0.309–1.017 crosses 1.0, which is exactly what a two-sided 95% interval keys on.
inferences.problem: The draft has already explained that the trial's prespecified analysis used a one-sided alpha of 0.10, not a two-sided alpha of 0.05. A two-sided 95% CI corresponds to a two-sided alpha of 0.05. The prespecified one-sided alpha of 0.10 corresponds to a two-sided 90% CI (or equivalently, a one-sided 95% CI). Saying the 95% CI 'is exactly what a two-sided 95% interval keys on' is correct as a description of what the Lancet paper reported, but the sentence implies this interval is the relevant inferential benchmark — when the trial's own registered threshold would correspond to a 90% two-sided CI. The draft's own p-value section explains the trial used a one-sided alpha of 0.10, making this sentence internally inconsistent with that explanation.
inferences.correct_reading: The 95% CI crossing 1.0 is consistent with a two-sided p > 0.05, which is how the Lancet paper presents it. But the trial's prespecified threshold was a one-sided alpha of 0.10, which corresponds to a two-sided 80% CI (or one-sided 90% CI) — not a two-sided 95% CI. The relevant inferential benchmark for this trial is not the 95% CI crossing 1.0.
inferences.fix: Replace 'The confidence interval is the tell: 0.309–1.017 crosses 1.0, which is exactly what a two-sided 95% interval keys on' with 'The 95% CI reported in the Lancet paper — 0.309–1.017 — crosses 1.0, consistent with the two-sided p of 0.053 the paper reports. But the trial's own prespecified threshold was a one-sided alpha of 0.10, against which 0.0266 was a clear pass; the 95% CI crossing 1.0 is the Lancet paper's framing, not the trial's registered one.'

inferences.quote: Adjuvant melanoma trials have a history of recurrence benefits that took years to translate into survival benefits, and sometimes never did.
inferences.problem: This sentence is accurate and appropriately hedged. No finding.
inferences.correct_reading: The sentence is accurate as written.

inferences.quote: For adjuvant PD-1 inhibitors specifically — the comparison arm in this very trial — in the three trials whose registry records we hold — KEYNOTE-054, KEYNOTE-716 and CheckMate 238 — none has reported a statistically significant overall survival benefit against placebo as a prespecified endpoint in its own population
inferences.problem: CheckMate 238 compares nivolumab to ipilimumab — it has no placebo arm. The draft acknowledges this immediately after ('CheckMate 238's arms are nivolumab and ipilimumab, so there is no placebo arm to report against'), but the sentence itself includes CheckMate 238 in a list of trials described as testing 'against placebo as a prespecified endpoint in its own population.' A reader quoting this sentence alone will take CheckMate 238 as a PD-1-vs-placebo trial that failed to show OS benefit, which is wrong on two counts: it is not a PD-1 inhibitor trial (nivolumab is PD-1, but the comparator is ipilimumab, a CTLA-4 inhibitor, not placebo), and the sentence's own framing ('against placebo') does not apply to it.
inferences.correct_reading: KEYNOTE-054 and KEYNOTE-716 are the relevant PD-1-vs-placebo trials. CheckMate 238 is a PD-1 vs CTLA-4 trial with no placebo arm and should not appear in a list qualified by 'against placebo.' The draft corrects this in the next sentence but the sentence itself is wrong.
inferences.fix: Remove CheckMate 238 from the parenthetical list: 'in the two trials whose registry records we hold — KEYNOTE-054 and KEYNOTE-716 — neither has reported a statistically significant overall survival benefit against placebo as a prespecified endpoint in its own population.' Then retain the existing note about CheckMate 238 separately.

inferences.quote: Reading only the first pair would tell you the added therapy costs nothing, and it does.
inferences.problem: The sentence is grammatically ambiguous: 'it does' could be read as 'it does cost nothing' (contradicting the intended meaning) or 'it does cost something' (the intended meaning). The intended reading is that the added therapy does carry a cost in grade 3+ adverse events, but the sentence construction invites the opposite reading.
inferences.correct_reading: The intended meaning is that the added therapy does carry a cost — grade 3 or worse treatment-related events were higher (25% vs 18%). The sentence should be rewritten to make this unambiguous.
inferences.fix: Replace 'Reading only the first pair would tell you the added therapy costs nothing, and it does' with 'Reading only the first pair would tell you the added therapy costs nothing in toxicity — but it does: grade 3 or worse treatment-related events were higher on the combination (25% vs 18%).'

inferences.quote: the 49% reduction in the hazard of recurrence or death, the 59% reduction in the hazard of distant metastasis or death, both from the five-year follow-up — describe a different trial: an open-label study of 157 patients
inferences.problem: The draft's own sources section confirms that the five-year KEYNOTE-942 data were published simultaneously in the Journal of Clinical Oncology and presented at ASCO 2026. The January 2026 topline release (also cited) reported the same HR=0.510 figure. The draft correctly attributes these to KEYNOTE-942. However, the phrase 'reduction in the hazard of recurrence or death' is the draft's own restatement of the companies' language 'reduction in the risk of recurrence or death.' The companies' language ('risk') is technically imprecise for a hazard ratio, but the draft's substitution of 'hazard' is the correct reading. This is not an error in the draft — it is the draft correcting the companies' language. No finding.
inferences.correct_reading: The draft's restatement is more precise than the companies' original language. No finding.

inferences.quote: Reported as a percentage that becomes 'a 49% reduction in the hazard of recurrence or death' — a correct restatement of the ratio, and still a relative rate rather than a share of patients spared.
inferences.problem: The draft defines this as a 'correct restatement' of HR 0.510. However, the companies' own language — and the language used in the five-year JCO paper and the ASCO 2026 release — is '49% reduction in the risk of recurrence or death,' not 'reduction in the hazard.' A hazard ratio is a ratio of hazard rates, not a risk ratio. The draft's own explainer section correctly distinguishes these: 'An HR of 0.51 does not mean 49% of patients were saved. It means that at any given moment during the trial, someone in the treatment group was recurring or dying at about half the rate.' Calling '49% reduction in the hazard' a 'correct restatement' of HR 0.510 is itself an approximation — the HR is a ratio of instantaneous rates, not a single percentage reduction — but it is the standard shorthand used in oncology and is defensible. No blocking finding.
inferences.correct_reading: The phrasing is standard oncology shorthand and defensible, though strictly the HR is a ratio of hazard rates rather than a single percentage reduction applicable at all time points.
inferences.fix: No change needed, or optionally add a parenthetical: '(a standard shorthand for the ratio of hazard rates, not a single percentage applicable at every moment of follow-up)'.

inferences.quote: It is manufactured per patient. The therapy is built from an individual tumour's own mutations, so it requires surgically removed tumour tissue and takes weeks to produce. That constrains who can realistically receive it even after approval.
inferences.problem: This sentence is accurate and appropriately hedged. No finding.

The arithmetic shown does not add up to 3.94. The six dimensions and their weights as stated in the scorecard are: Source quality 3/5 (weight 0.25), Data support 1/5 (weight 0.20), Reproducibility 4/5 (weight 0.20), Consensus 4/5 (weight 0.15), Recency 5/5 (weight 0.10), Rigor 5/5 (weight 0.10). The 'Is the effect real?' score excludes Data support (weight 0.20) and uses the remaining five dimensions. The formula shown is (3×.25 + 4×.20 + 4×.15 + 5×.10 + 5×.10) ÷ .80. Computing: (0.75 + 0.80 + 0.60 + 0.50 + 0.50) ÷ 0.80 = 3.15 ÷ 0.80 = 3.9375 ≈ 3.94. The arithmetic is correct. However, the weights assigned in the formula (0.25, 0.20, 0.15, 0.10, 0.10) sum to 0.80, which matches the divisor. But the rubric lists six dimensions with weights that must sum to 1.0. If the six weights are 0.25, 0.20, 0.20, 0.15, 0.10, 0.10 (summing to 1.0), then the 'Is the effect real?' score excludes Data support (0.20) and the remaining weights sum to 0.80 — consistent. The arithmetic checks out. No finding.

inferences.quote: the trial's own threshold is on the record: the three-year paper says the trial was designed with approximately 80% power to detect a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.5 against a one-sided alpha of 0.10
inferences.problem: This describes KEYNOTE-942 (the Phase 2b), not INTerpath-001 (the Phase 3). The sentence appears in the p-value section discussing the KEYNOTE-942 primary analysis p-values (0.0266 one-sided, 0.053 two-sided). The referent 'this trial' is KEYNOTE-942, and the three-year paper cited is the JCO Oncology Advances paper about KEYNOTE-942. This is correct in context. However, the section heading is about p-values generally, and a reader could mistake 'this trial's own threshold' as referring to INTerpath-001. The draft does not state INTerpath-001's prespecified alpha, which is not publicly available from the sources cited. No factual error, but the referent could be clearer.
inferences.correct_reading: The threshold described (one-sided alpha of 0.10) belongs to KEYNOTE-942, not INTerpath-001. The draft's context makes this clear to a careful reader but the referent 'this trial' is ambiguous at the sentence level.
inferences.fix: Replace 'this trial's own threshold' with 'KEYNOTE-942's own threshold'.

inferences.quote: 0.0266 was inside its own prespecified threshold by a wide margin
inferences.problem: The prespecified one-sided alpha for KEYNOTE-942 was 0.10. A p-value of 0.0266 is inside that threshold (0.0266 < 0.10), but whether 'by a wide margin' is warranted depends on context. The ratio is about 3.75-fold below the threshold, which is a meaningful margin. This is a defensible characterisation. No blocking finding.
inferences.correct_reading: 0.0266 is well below the prespecified one-sided alpha of 0.10. 'Wide margin' is defensible.

inferences.quote: Whether anyone lives longer, and by how much. The only survival figure in the programme is descriptive and rests on fourteen deaths; its interval, 0.165 to 1.345, is too wide to separate a large benefit from a small harm. The question is open, not answered either way.
inferences.problem: This sentence correctly avoids the MISSING_NUMBER_AS_MISSING_EVIDENCE error and correctly avoids the RATIO_AS_LIVES error. It accurately describes the interval as spanning from a large benefit to a small harm. No finding.

inferences.quote: in the study will continue in order to evaluate other key secondary endpoints, including overall survival
inferences.problem: This is the same finding as finding #4 above (the ASCO Post quote). The draft quotes this sentence from the ASCO Post article as if it accurately describes the trial's endpoint hierarchy. The trial protocol (NCT05933577, JCO abstract) lists OS as a secondary endpoint, not a key secondary endpoint. DMFS was the designated key secondary. Quoting the ASCO Post's 'key secondary endpoints, including overall survival' without correction implicitly endorses the characterisation.
inferences.correct_reading: OS is a secondary endpoint in INTerpath-001, not a key secondary endpoint. The key secondary endpoint was DMFS, which was met. The ASCO Post's phrasing overstates OS's pre-specified hierarchical status.
inferences.fix: Add a parenthetical correction after the quote: '(the trial protocol lists OS as a secondary endpoint; DMFS was the designated key secondary)'.

Also noted the double-blind design eliminates open-label assessment bias as an explanation for the directional result, while correctly flagging that magnitude cannot be assessed.

contradictions.quote: MLQ News: The companies have not disclosed hazard ratios, confidence intervals, p-values, median follow-up or event counts for the Phase 3 trial.
contradictions.counterexample: MLQ News actually states: 'The companies have not disclosed the Phase 3 hazard ratios, p-values, median follow-up or detailed adverse-event rates.' The words 'confidence intervals' and 'event counts' do not appear in the MLQ text found; the draft's quoted version adds two items MLQ did not enumerate.
contradictions.fix: Quote MLQ only for what it actually said: that hazard ratios, p-values, median follow-up, and detailed adverse-event rates were not disclosed. The confidence-interval and event-count items in the quoted sentence belong to the draft's own analysis, not to MLQ, and should be attributed accordingly.

contradictions.quote: One detail has had little attention. Merck's own description of the Phase 3 defines its primary endpoint as recurrence 'as assessed by the investigator' rather than by central adjudication.
contradictions.counterexample: The ASCO Post explicitly states: 'The primary endpoint was recurrence-free survival, defined as the time from randomization to any disease recurrence... as assessed by the investigator, or death due to any cause.' Cancer Therapy Advisor states the same language verbatim. Both pieces published this detail at the time of the announcement.
contradictions.fix: Reframe as: 'The investigator-assessed endpoint definition appeared in the ASCO Post and Cancer Therapy Advisor, though neither piece discussed what it implies about assessment bias in the context of the double-blind design.' The claim of 'little attention' is overstated; the detail was printed, just not analysed.

contradictions.quote: Every outlet whose article we hold attributed those figures correctly to KEYNOTE-942 — The ASCO Post, Dermatology Times, Practical Dermatology, KOL Pulse and MLQ News
contradictions.counterexample: OncoDaily, Biotech Blueprint, AJMC, CancerNetwork, BioPharm International, EMJ Reviews, and Pharmacy Times also attributed the figures correctly to KEYNOTE-942 (or omitted them entirely). The list of five outlets understates the breadth of correct attribution and could imply the others did not get it right.
contradictions.fix: Expand the list or use a formulation such as 'every specialist outlet we reviewed' rather than naming only five, to avoid implying the unnamed outlets failed on attribution.

contradictions.quote: The third figure has not come back. We also removed a 'five-year topline of 20 January 2026' reporting a one-sided nominal p = 0.0075. That document is still in nothing we hold and in no source list on this page, and nothing found since has changed that.
contradictions.counterexample: The January 20, 2026 Moderna/Merck press release is publicly available (Moderna IR PDF, s2.q4cdn.com) and reports 'one-sided nominal p=0.0075' for the five-year KEYNOTE-942 RFS analysis. CancerNetwork also cites this p-value from the five-year data. The document exists and is findable; the draft's correction notice implies it may not.
contradictions.fix: The correction note should be updated: the January 20, 2026 release exists and is publicly available. The p=0.0075 figure is real and sourced. The draft should either add this document to its source list or explain why it is choosing not to rely on it, rather than leaving a reader to infer the document may be fictitious.

coverage.what_this_piece_can_add: No outlet found — including the most careful specialist treatments — explains the OS confidence interval (0.165–1.345) in terms of what its two ends mean in plain language, or connects the n=14 death count to the interval width in a way a non-specialist reader can use. The draft's walk-through of that interval, and its explanation of why 'an encouraging trend' is the only honest label for a result that spans an 84% reduction to a 35% increase, is genuinely absent from all coverage found and is the layer this piece adds that even the best specialist reporting does not.
